lines.say: Suppose a friend secretly sets up a qubit, which reads zero or one when checked. Can you tell how?
You measure it, which means you look, and it reads zero. What did you learn?
Almost nothing. One measurement gives one bit, a single zero or one.
That zero could come from a qubit that nearly always reads zero, or rarely does.
It's like an opinion poll. One voter can't tell you who will win.
But ask a thousand, and the percentages come into focus.
Quantum programs do the same. They set up the qubit identically again and again, measuring it each time.
Each run is called a shot, and each shot is one vote.
Say your friend's qubit reads zero three times out of four.
Ten shots might give six zeros: sixty percent, not seventy five.
A hundred shots give seventy one zeros. A thousand give seven hundred and forty eight.
The fraction wobbles at first, then settles toward the true odds.
To halve the wobble, you need four times the shots.
So when a fifty fifty qubit gives five hundred and twelve zeros and four hundred and eighty eight ones, relax.
Nothing is broken. That gap is called shot noise, the normal wobble of any poll.
Here's where the poll breaks down. A voter already had an opinion before you asked.
But our qubit has no answer waiting. Measuring creates one, and leaves the qubit sitting on it.
That's why every vote needs a freshly prepared qubit.
One shot is one vote, and many shots reveal the odds.
